I am sixty years old, and I have farmed these fields in Quzhou my whole life. My family holds seven mu of good flat land on the North China Plain. My children have gone to work in the city, so it is just me and my wife now. I do not have the back or the patience to learn new crops at my age, and I do not want to take risks with vegetables that might rot if the price drops. The wheat–maize rotation is what I know, and the machinery teams come right to my door for planting and harvest.

This year I will plant **winter wheat** on all seven mu in early October and follow it with **summer maize** planted immediately after the wheat harvest in mid-June. I will use **improved wheat varieties** like *Shimai 22* or *Liangxing 77* and **hybrid maize** like *Nongda 372* or *Denghai 605*. These seeds cost more, but they are reliable and give me the yields I need. I buy them from the township supply shop.

For the wheat, I will spread about **50 kg per mu of compound fertilizer** (18-22-5 or 15-15-15) as a basal dressing before sowing, using the rotary tiller to work it into the soil. At the jointing stage in spring I will top-dress with urea. For the maize, I will use **no-tillage** after the wheat harvest—there is no time to waste in June—and put down about **40 kg per mu of compound fertilizer** (28-6-6 or 26-8-8) at planting. I will irrigate the wheat three times (overwintering, jointing, and grain-filling) and the maize twice if the summer rains are short. Water is getting tight, so I try not to waste it.

I will spray herbicide once for each crop, and add fungicide and insecticide when the neighbors start spraying—about four times for wheat and three or four times for maize. I aim for around **1,000 jin per mu of wheat** and a bit more for maize if the weather holds.
